questions.stem: A 50-year-old patient admitted with STEMI, now status-post CABG, and with a complicated hospital course thereafter, including prolonged respiratory failure requiring tracheostomy and gastrostomy tube placements, who also received several days of broad-spectrum antibiotics postoperatively because of shock, and concern for possible sepsis, is now having increasing supplemental oxygen requirement and fever. His chest radiograph shows diffuse pulmonary opacities, worst in the right-lower lobe. His nurse also has noted increasingly profuse and purulent tracheal secretions. He was started on linezolid and meropenem, but after 2 days he was still having fevers, and his respiratory status continued to worsen. Tracheal aspirate culture is now growing an organism that was identified as an oxidase-positive, nonfermenting gram-negative bacillus.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.explanation: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia This patient has hospital-acquired pneumonia and did not demonstrate clinical improvement on broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy. He has multiple risk factors for development of drug-resistant pathogens, including his prolonged ICU stay and antecedent antibiotic therapy. Linezolid and meropenem would provide more than adequate activity against most gram-positive and gram-negative pathogens, including those that would produce extended-spectrum β-lactamases. Stenotrophomonas can be a cause of HAP , is intrinsically resistant to the antibiotic agents that he has been receiving, and is a nonfermenting gram-negative bacillus that is oxidase-positive. Other nonfermenting, oxidase-positive gram-negative bacilli include Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Achromobacter, and Burkholderia, among others.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q31

questions.question: State the shortest appropriate treatment duration for each of the following infections.
questions.model_answer: a) Cellulitis: 5 days (extend only if not improving). b) Acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis: 5 days (levofloxacin) – 7 days for ciprofloxacin. c) CAP: minimum 5 days (afebrile 48–72 h, clinically stable). d) VAP: 7 days. e) Frontal brain abscess: 6–8 weeks of IV therapy is traditional; a shorter 3–4 week course may be adequate when the abscess has been surgically excised.
questions.beyond_mandell: Durations for cellulitis, pyelonephritis, CAP and VAP are from IDSA guidance (IDSA SSTI 2014; IDSA/ATS HAP/VAP 2016; IDSA/ATS CAP 2019), not this chapter.

questions.question: For each of the following conditions, list the shortest effective duration of antibiotics: retropharyngeal abscess (pediatric), ventilator-associated pneumonia (adult), community-acquired pneumonia, cellulitis, and uncomplicated pyelonephritis.
questions.question_raw: For the following conditions, list the shortest effective duration of antibiotics: Retropharyngeal abscess on Peds exam, VAP on adult exam, CAP, Cellulitis, Uncomplicated pyelonephritis.

parts.text: For each condition, list the shortest effective duration of antibiotics.

parts_raw.text: For each condition, list the shortest effective duration of antibiotics.

questions.model_answer: (1) Retropharyngeal abscess (peds): ~14 days total (with surgical drainage as needed). (2) VAP: 7 days. (3) CAP: 5 days (minimum, provided clinically stable/afebrile 48-72 h). (4) Cellulitis: 5 days (uncomplicated, extend if not improving). (5) Uncomplicated pyelonephritis: 7 days (fluoroquinolone, e.g. ciprofloxacin; levofloxacin 750 mg can be 5 days where local resistance <10%).
questions.beyond_mandell: Durations are not specified in this chapter; from IDSA/ATS CAP (2019), IDSA/ATS HAP/VAP (2016), IDSA SSTI (2014) and IDSA uncomplicated cystitis/pyelonephritis (2011) guidelines.

cohort_answer.text: Retropharyngeal abscess 14 days (UTD, Redbook); VAP 7 days; CAP 5 days; Cellulitis 5 days; Uncomplicated pyelo 7 days. Resource: AMMI Duration Paper https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9615468/

questions.question: A patient in the ICU develops ventilator-associated pneumonia. A BAL sample grows Stenotrophomonas maltophilia resistant to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
questions.question_raw: A patient in the ICU develops a ventilator-associated pneumonia. BAL sample grows Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, resistant to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

parts.text: Name four treatments, each from a different antimicrobial class, that can be used for this infection.

parts_raw.text: Name FOUR treatments (each from different antimicrobial classes) that can be used for this infection? – (2016; 2019)

questions.model_answer: (1) Fluoroquinolone: levofloxacin. (2) Tetracycline: minocycline (or tigecycline). (3) Siderophore cephalosporin: cefiderocol. (4) Beta-lactam/beta-lactamase-inhibitor plus monobactam combination: ceftazidime-avibactam with aztreonam.
questions.beyond_mandell: IDSA 2023 guidance on antimicrobial-resistant gram-negative infections (Stenotrophomonas maltophilia).

questions.question: Write the shortest duration of therapy for ventilator-associated pneumonia, community-acquired pneumonia, cellulitis, and uncomplicated pyelonephritis.
questions.question_raw: Write the shortest duration of therapy for VAP, CAP, Cellulitis, Uncomplicated Pyelo
questions.model_answer: a) VAP: 7 days. b) CAP: 5 days (minimum, once afebrile and clinically stable 48-72 h). c) Cellulitis: 5 days (uncomplicated). d) Uncomplicated pyelonephritis: 7 days with a fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 750 mg for 5 days where local resistance <10%; 10-14 days for beta-lactams/TMP-SMX).
questions.beyond_mandell: Durations not in this chapter; from IDSA/ATS VAP (2016, 7 days), IDSA/ATS CAP (2019, minimum 5 days), IDSA SSTI (2014) and IDSA pyelonephritis (2011) guidelines.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort's 3-day durations for VAP and CAP are not guideline-endorsed: IDSA/ATS recommend 7 days for VAP and a minimum of 5 days for CAP.

cohort_answer.text: VAP: 3 days (IDSA 2016). CAP: 3 days (IDSA 2019). Cellulitis: 5 days (IDSA 2014). Uncomplicated pyelonephritis: 5 days (IDSA 2010; fluoroquinolones only for 5d if local resistance <10%).

questions.question: An intubated patient develops ventilator-associated pneumonia due to Stenotrophomonas maltophilia and is currently on meropenem.
questions.question_raw: There is a patient who is intubated and develops VAP due to Stenotrophomonas (severity not specified). He is on Meropenem.

parts.text: What is the best empiric therapy for this infection?
He is unable to tolerate that drug. Name two non-beta-lactam antibiotic alternatives you can use that have relatively little toxicity.

parts_raw.text: What is the best empiric therapy for this infection?
He is unable to tolerate that drug. Name two non-beta lactam antibiotic alternatives you can use that have relatively little toxicity

questions.model_answer:
a) Stenotrophomonas maltophilia is intrinsically resistant to carbapenems. It carries two chromosomally encoded beta-lactamases: the L1 metallo-beta-lactamase (zinc-dependent) hydrolyzes penicillins, cephalosporins, and carbapenems, and the L2 serine beta-lactamase hydrolyzes aztreonam and extended-spectrum cephalosporins. Meropenem is therefore predictably inactive.
b) High-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the drug of choice and best empiric agent; for critically ill/severe infection IDSA 2023 favors combination therapy using two active agents (e.g., TMP-SMX plus minocycline or levofloxacin).
c) (1) Levofloxacin (fluoroquinolone). (2) Minocycline (tetracycline). Both are well tolerated relative to alternatives such as tigecycline.
questions.beyond_mandell: Provided context text is Mandell Ch. 221 (Burkholderia pseudomallei/mallei) and does not cover Stenotrophomonas; answer rests on IDSA 2023 Guidance on AMR Gram-negative infections.

cohort_answer.text: Meropenem inappropriate: Intrinsic resistance (L1 metallo beta-lactamase); S. maltophilia carries numerous resistance genes/mutations - L1 hydrolyzes penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems (not aztreonam), L2 has extended cephalosporin activity and hydrolyzes aztreonam; intrinsic aminoglycoside resistance via chromosomal acetyl transferase enzymes; multidrug efflux pumps reduce TMP-SMX, tetracycline, fluoroquinolone activity, chromosomal Smqnr genes further reduce fluoroquinolone effectiveness. Best empiric therapy (IDSA 2023 Guidance): 1) Use of 2 agents: TMP-SMX, minocycline/tigecycline, cefiderocol or levofloxacin; 2) Combination of ceftazidime-avibactam and aztreonam when significant instability or intolerance/inactivity of other agents identified. Alternatives if intolerant: Levofloxacin; Minocycline > Tigecycline
